analysis.one_liner: Raises tobacco taxes and spends the money expanding Medicaid for children and pregnant women.
analysis.headline: The bill would have quadrupled the federal cigarette tax, from 12.5 cents to 50 cents a pack, to fund Medicaid coverage for low-income families, but no committee ever held a hearing or vote and it died when the 103rd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: H.R. 1246 would have sharply raised federal excise taxes on cigarettes, cigars, and other tobacco products, with the cigarette tax jumping from 12.5 cents to 50 cents per pack and rates rising with inflation each year. The new revenue would have gone into a dedicated trust fund: 80% to expand Medicaid to children up to age 19 and pregnant women in families earning up to twice the poverty line, plus smaller shares for health programs, youth anti-smoking campaigns, payments to states, and aid to tobacco farmers switching to other crops. The bill never received a hearing or vote in any of the three House committees it was sent to.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income uninsured families: children up to age 19 and pregnant women in households earning up to 200% of the poverty line would gain Medicaid coverage, and the federal government would pay 100% of the new cost so states would not have to. Hospitals and physicians gain from required minimum Medicaid payment rates tied to Medicare rates, funded federally. Community health programs, lead poisoning prevention, AIDS prevention, and youth anti-smoking campaigns gain dedicated funding. State and local governments gain grants compensating for tax revenue lost to reduced smoking, and tobacco farmers gain offset payments and crop-conversion help.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low-income uninsured children and pregnant women

how_it_helps.text: Expands Medicaid to children up to age 19 and pregnant women in families with incomes up to 200% of the poverty line, and extends a smaller expansion to other adults under 65, with no asset test and a simplified income calculation.
Dedicates 80% of the new tobacco tax revenue to the Medicaid expansion and requires the federal government to pay 100% of the new costs, so states face no new financial burden.

Sets federal floors on what states must pay hospitals and physicians for Medicaid care, rising toward Medicare-rate levels by the late 1990s, which supporters argued would keep doctors from turning away Medicaid patients.

Funds lead poisoning prevention, minority health programs, AIDS prevention, community health centers, the National Health Service Corps, and public anti-smoking campaigns aimed especially at keeping young people from starting to smoke.
Sends 10% of the money to state and local governments to replace tax revenue lost when smoking declines, and 3% to tobacco farmers as offset payments and grants to convert to other crops.

analysis.who_pays: Smokers pay through much higher tobacco taxes — the cigarette tax would have gone from 12.5 cents to 50 cents per pack, with similar increases on cigars, smokeless, and pipe tobacco — and because tobacco taxes are flat per-pack charges, they take a bigger share of income from low-income smokers. Tobacco companies lose sales as prices rise and consumption falls, and tobacco farmers face reduced demand, though the bill compensates them with payments and crop-transition aid. Retailers holding old inventory would have owed a one-time floor stock tax due by June 30, 1994.
analysis.who_pays_short: Smokers, tobacco companies, and tobacco farmers

drawbacks.text: The cigarette tax would have quadrupled from 12.5 cents to 50 cents per pack, and because excise taxes are flat per pack, the burden falls hardest on low-income smokers, the same income group the Medicaid expansion targets.
The Medicaid expansion is capped at whatever the tobacco tax fund yields, and as the tax discourages smoking the revenue base shrinks — so coverage depends on a funding stream designed to dry up.

Requiring states to raise Medicaid payment rates toward Medicare levels pushes up the cost of the program, and while the bill pays those increases at 100% federal share initially, that commitment competes with the eligibility expansion for the same limited fund.
The one-time floor stock tax on tobacco already in warehouses and stores, due June 30, 1994, would have hit small retailers and distributors holding inventory.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is a regressive tax on a product that kills people, spent on health coverage for poor families and on programs that keep kids from smoking — a trade most public-health advocates consider favorable, and the bill's own farmer-transition and state-compensation funds acknowledge the distributional costs. The design weakness is real: tying an entitlement expansion to a revenue source meant to shrink as consumption falls made the coverage promise uncertain over time, and the provider payment floors added a large, open-ended claim on the same fund. Still, as written, the gains to uninsured low-income families outweigh the costs to smokers and the tobacco industry.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in three House committees and their subcommittees for nearly two years and never got a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Michael Andrews introduced the bill on March 8, 1993, with five original cosponsors including one Republican, and it was referred jointly to the Ways and Means, Energy and Commerce, and Agriculture Committees.
Within three weeks each committee had passed it down to a subcommittee — Specialty Crops and Natural Resources, Health, and Health and the Environment — where no action was ever recorded.
Eleven members cosponsored the bill, 9 Democrats and 2 Republicans, but no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever took place before the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tobacco companies were the clearest winners: they avoided a fourfold cigarette tax increase, an inflation-locked tax schedule, and federally funded counter-advertising aimed at their future customers. Hospitals and physicians also lost the guaranteed Medicaid payment floors, and low-income uninsured families got nothing from a Congress that produced no major health coverage expansion in 1993-94.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's 12 sponsors included 10 Democrats and 2 Republicans, but no chamber ever voted on it, so there is no roll-call record, and the Democratic-led committees that held the bill never acted.

industries.note: The bill would have quadrupled the cigarette excise tax, raised rates on every other tobacco product, locked in annual inflation increases, taxed roll-your-own cigarette tobacco for the first time, and funded counter-advertising aimed at youths. Its interest ran directly against the public-health purpose of the bill.

Higher taxes were expected to cut domestic tobacco consumption, reducing demand for leaf — but the bill dedicated 3% of the fund to offset payments to farmers and grants to help them and their states convert to other crops.

The bill set federal floors on Medicaid payment rates for inpatient hospital and physician services, rising toward Medicare-rate levels, and paid the increases at 100% federal share. More covered patients plus guaranteed payment rates would have meant more revenue for providers serving low-income communities.
